targets.html:
Your forecast says 120 appointments next month. Your break-even point is 80. The margin of safety is the 40 appointments you can lose before the operating plan reaches zero profit, assuming prices and costs hold. It is a useful risk check when one client cancels, the season softens or a promotion changes what you collect. It is not a guarantee that the next 40 cancellations will have identical costs.

Work from a break-even point you can audit

Imagine a US appointment-based service. One completed appointment collects an illustrative $150. Job-specific labor, materials, transaction fees and travel total $75, leaving $75 contribution. Monthly fixed costs, including planned owner pay, are $6,000. The break-even point is $6,000 ÷ $75 = 80 completed appointments. Those 80 appointments produce 80 × $150 = $12,000 sales. OpenStax explains the margin-of-safety and operating-leverage framework; the numbers here are our own fictional planning example.

One-month calculation Formula Result
Contribution per appointment $150 − $75 $75
Break-even appointments $6,000 ÷ $75 80
Break-even sales 80 × $150 $12,000
Forecast appointments and sales 120 × $150 120 and $18,000
Margin of safety in units 120 − 80 40 appointments
Margin of safety in sales $18,000 − $12,000 $6,000
Margin of safety ratio $6,000 ÷ $18,000 33.33%

Audit it through profit: 120 × $75 = $9,000 contribution, and $9,000 − $6,000 fixed costs = $3,000 operating profit. If volume falls by 40 appointments, contribution falls by 40 × $75 = $3,000 and profit reaches zero. This is why the dollar cushion is sales revenue, not $3,000 profit. Do not subtract the $6,000 fixed cost again from the $6,000 sales cushion.

Our break-even analysis example helps if the 80-appointment threshold itself needs work. The fixed-versus-variable costs guide helps classify expenses before using them in either calculation.

Which sales number belongs in the numerator?

For a completed month, use actual collected or recognized sales consistently with the costs for that same month. For a future month, label the figure a forecast margin of safety. Do not present a forecast as a measured result. If you have 120 bookings but only 110 are likely to be completed after expected cancellations, the prudent forecast starts with 110, not the calendar total.

The ratio's denominator is current or forecast sales, not break-even sales.

In this example $6,000 ÷ $18,000 is 33.33%; $6,000 ÷ $12,000 would answer a different question. If you report units instead, 40 ÷ 120 also gives 33.33% because all appointments have the same $150 price. With varied services, a simple count percentage can disagree with the sales-dollar percentage. Give the period, price mix and unit of measure beside the number.

This operating cushion does not include everything that can threaten cash. A customer might pay late, a supplier might require an early deposit, or the owner may need to replace equipment. The monthly expense budget guide illustrates why a business needs cash planning alongside its operating threshold. Margin of safety measures distance from modeled break-even under stated assumptions; it is not a bank balance.

Margin of safety percentage formula: choose the sales denominator

Three ways to read the same sales cushion
MeasureUseful forCheck first
Jobs or unitsBooking losses and workloadServices must have comparable contribution.
Sales dollarsRevenue changes across periodsUse the same price and mix as the break-even calculation.
PercentageComparing months of different sizesDivide the gap by actual or forecast sales, not break-even sales.

A forecast cushion depends on the forecast; it is not cash in the bank or a probability of success. Label whether the threshold covers overhead only or also owner pay and a profit goal. The OpenStax accounting definitions distinguish contribution from the sales gap above break-even.

Three changes that shrink the cushion

Keep the original 120-appointment forecast unless the scenario says otherwise. These cases change one driver at a time:

Illustrative case Break-even appointments Forecast appointments Unit cushion Profit after fixed costs
Base: $150 price, $75 cost, $6,000 fixed 80 120 40 $3,000
20% fewer completed appointments 80 96 16 $1,200
Fixed costs rise to $7,500 100 120 20 $1,500
Price drops to $135, job cost stays $75 100 120 20 $1,200

In the 20% volume-drop case, 96 × $75 − $6,000 = $1,200 profit. Sixteen appointments remain above break-even; the new unit cushion is 16 ÷ 96 = 16.67% of completed appointments. If volume falls by 35% from 120 to 78, the model loses 2 × $75 = $150 because 78 × $75 − $6,000 = −$150.

The higher-fixed-cost case breaks even at $7,500 ÷ $75 = 100 appointments. Profit at 120 becomes $9,000 − $7,500 = $1,500. The discount case has $135 − $75 = $60 contribution, so $6,000 ÷ $60 = 100 appointments, with $1,200 profit at 120. Its dollar margin of safety is 20 × $135 = $2,700, not 20 × $150. Recalculate dollars after any price change.

These scenarios assume one comparable service and enough hours for 120 appointments. A new guaranteed staff shift at 110 bookings would change fixed costs. A promotion that attracts lower-margin services would change the average contribution. Model those steps and mixes before treating a single safety percentage as a forecast.

Turn a cushion into an operating decision

A 40-appointment cushion can guide how much booking volatility the plan can absorb. Compare it with your own monthly range of completed work, cancellations and repeat-customer concentration. If one commercial client accounts for 30 appointments, losing that account would use three quarters of the 40-appointment unit cushion, even if you retain the other clients. That observation is more actionable than a generic “safe” percentage.

If the forecast depends on a promotion, ask what the promotion does to both volume and contribution. If it cuts $15 from the $150 price but produces ten more appointments, the break-even threshold rises as shown above.

Ten more appointments at $60 contribution add $600, but the discount applies to all eligible sales in the scenario. Model the full changed mix rather than adding $600 to the old profit result. A cushion can shrink even as the calendar fills.

If actual volume is close to break-even, reducing rework, filling cancellations and protecting the average collected price may matter sooner than renting more space. The lower your break-even point guide covers interventions; margin of safety gives you a way to measure the room available before an intervention is urgent.

Interpret a negative margin of safety correctly

Keep the guide's $12,000 break-even revenue and suppose actual sales are 78 jobs at $150, or $11,700. Dollar margin of safety is $11,700 − $12,000 = −$300. Percentage margin of safety is −$300 ÷ $11,700 × 100 = −2.56%. There is no sales-loss cushion: the business is below the modeled threshold.

With $75 contribution per job and an 80-job break-even point, the two-job shortfall produces a $150 loss under that cost boundary. The $300 revenue gap is not itself the profit loss, because selling those two jobs would also incur variable costs.

Show actual and forecast cushions separately. A forecast of 120 jobs cannot erase a shortfall in the completed period. If actual sales are zero, percentage margin of safety is undefined because the denominator is zero; report the dollar gap and explain the missing percentage rather than displaying 0% or an infinite cushion.

Margin of safety in units: keep fractional and whole thresholds distinct

A separate fictional business sells 200 units at $50 each, with $20 variable cost per unit and $4,000 fixed costs. Exact operating break-even is 133.3333 units. Its formula-based margin of safety is 200 − 133.3333 = 66.6667 units, or 33.3333% of current unit sales. The practical minimum is 134 whole sales, so only 66 whole sales can be lost while staying at or above that whole-unit requirement.

At 134 sales the operating result is $20; at 133 it is −$10. Rounding the cushion to 67 and calling it safe would therefore be misleading. Use an unchanged price, variable rate and sales mix for this sensitivity. The exact-versus-whole sales explanation shows the financial threshold and operational rounding separately.

Turn the margin of safety ratio into a sales alert

A percentage can become a review trigger. In a separate fictional month, break-even sales are $30,000 and forecast sales are $45,000. The cushion is $15,000, or 33.33% of forecast sales. A chosen 20% cushion requires sales of $30,000 ÷ (1 − 0.20) = $37,500. The 20% is a management assumption, not a recommended universal buffer.

If the sales forecast falls to $36,000 with the same cost behavior, the cushion is $6,000 ÷ $36,000 = 16.67%. That crosses the chosen alert threshold even though forecast sales remain above break-even. Review the cause and cash calendar before deciding on a price or staffing change.

Recalculate break-even when contribution, fixed commitments or product mix changes. Do not preserve an old $30,000 threshold after a cost increase. With zero sales the percentage is undefined; show the dollar shortfall. A forecast cushion describes the assumptions, not evidence that those sales will occur.

Check the operating break-even calculation

Method reference, reviewed October 22, 2026. The worked figures in this section are separate fictional assumptions.

How to run your own numbers

Enter your average collected price, comparable job-linked costs and monthly fixed costs in the MyBreakeven general calculator. Compare its break-even volume with your own actual or credible forecast and calculate the unit and sales-dollar gap. The calculator supports other currencies; this US-dollar example is only an arithmetic illustration.

Common mistakes

Dividing by break-even sales for the percentage. The margin of safety ratio compares the gap with actual or forecast sales for the same period.

Mixing booked and completed appointments. A cancellation-free calendar can exaggerate the cushion. Track completed work and show how expected cancellations affect the forecast.

Using one price for unlike services. Forty standard appointments and forty premium jobs do not create the same sales-dollar cushion. Use a weighted mix or separate models.

Keeping the old break-even point after a discount. The $15 lower price changes contribution and raises required volume even if fixed costs stay put.

Calling the dollar cushion profit. $6,000 is sales above the break-even sales threshold; only its contribution portion becomes profit under the assumptions.

Ignoring a fixed-cost step. A bigger room, vehicle or guaranteed shift can move the break-even threshold when volume crosses a capacity boundary.

FAQs

Can margin of safety be negative?

Yes. If actual or forecast sales fall below break-even, the difference is negative and the model predicts an operating shortfall. Report the sign rather than displaying zero, then calculate how many additional sales or cost changes would close the gap.

Is margin of safety the same as contribution margin?

No. Contribution margin is what one sale or a group of sales leaves after variable costs. Margin of safety is the gap between actual or forecast sales and break-even sales. Contribution determines the break-even threshold used in the safety calculation.

Should I use units, dollars or a percentage?

Use units for staffing and booking decisions when jobs are comparable. Use dollars when prices or service types vary. A percentage helps compare periods of different sizes, but always keep the dollar or unit gap beside it.

What if my service mix changes during the month?

Recalculate the weighted contribution and break-even threshold. A simple unit-count cushion based on an old mix can mislead when customers shift toward lower-priced or more costly services.

Does a 33% margin of safety mean I can lose 33% of customers?

Only under the simplified case where each lost appointment has the same price and variable cost and fixed costs do not change. Losing a large client, a premium package or a route-dense cluster may have a different effect. Use the actual contribution of what you expect to lose.

Is a larger margin of safety always better?

It generally means more modeled distance from break-even under the same assumptions, but it may reflect an optimistic forecast. Compare the gap with real sales variability, cash timing and capacity before making a decision.

What to keep on your monthly page

  • Label actual versus forecast sales and use the same period as fixed costs.
  • Calculate the break-even point from contribution, then the unit and dollar gap.
  • Divide the dollar gap by actual or forecast sales for the percentage.
  • Rerun the model when price, service mix, staffing or overhead changes.

Margin of safety formulas: dollars, units and percentage

  • Sales dollars: actual or forecast sales − break-even sales.
  • Units: actual or forecast units sold − break-even units.
  • Percentage: (actual or forecast sales − break-even sales) ÷ actual or forecast sales × 100.

In the fictional USD example below, $18,000 forecast sales − $12,000 break-even sales = $6,000 sales cushion. Divide $6,000 by $18,000, not $12,000: the margin of safety is 33.33%, or 40 of 120 comparable appointments. This is a forecast cushion under the stated cost assumptions, not $6,000 profit or cash.

Use the same period and sales mix. Percentage margin of safety needs positive actual or forecast sales; at zero sales, report the dollar gap separately instead of dividing by zero. Follow the break-even and profit reconciliation.

targets.html:
Fixed costs stay constant in total for a stated period and relevant activity range. Variable costs change with a specified driver: units produced, jobs completed or payments processed. Fixed cost per unit falls as activity rises; variable cost per unit is constant only under a linear-rate assumption. Split mixed bills and model capacity steps before calculating contribution or break-even.

Reviewed November 13, 2026. Definitions and formulas were checked against the OpenStax managerial-accounting references below. All business amounts are fictional USD examples, not surveyed prices, industry benchmarks or your business’s results. State one period, activity driver and operating range before using a figure.

Quick answer: Fixed costs do not change in total when sales volume changes, such as rent or a software subscription. Variable costs change with each unit sold, such as ingredients, packaging, or sales commissions. Add fixed costs to find your operating base; subtract variable cost per sale from price to see what each sale contributes toward profit.

Fixed vs variable costs: compare total cost and cost per unit

Cost behavior within one stated period and relevant activity range
QuestionFixed costVariable cost
What happens to the total?Unchanged within the stated rangeChanges with the matching activity driver
What happens per unit?Falls as the same commitment is spread over more unitsConstant only under a linear per-unit assumption
At zero activity?The commitment can remain payableZero for a purely volume-driven cost; check minimum commitments
Typical conditional examplesA monthly premises lease or guaranteed salaryMaterial consumed, per-order packaging or a sales commission

Choose the driver before assigning a label: units produced, jobs completed, miles driven and sales dollars are different measures. A percentage card fee varies with collected revenue, so a discount can change its dollar cost per order. Fixed does not mean permanent, and variable does not mean discretionary. Both labels describe behavior over a defined time and range.

Total fixed cost formula and variable cost per unit

Reconciled formulas using the existing 80-visit fictional example, USD
MeasureFormulaWorked result
Total variable costVariable cost per visit × completed visits$81 × 80 = $6,480
Total costTotal fixed cost + total variable cost$3,200 + $6,480 = $9,680
Total fixed costTotal cost − total variable cost$9,680 − $6,480 = $3,200
Variable cost per unitTotal variable cost ÷ matching units$6,480 ÷ 80 = $81 per visit
Fixed cost per unitTotal fixed cost ÷ matching units$3,200 ÷ 80 = $40 per visit
Average total cost per unitTotal cost ÷ matching units$9,680 ÷ 80 = $121 per visit

The subtraction formula works only when total cost and variable cost cover the same costs, activity and period. It does not identify cost behavior from one unexplained bill. For total fixed cost = total cost − (variable cost per unit × units), independently establish the per-unit rate first. At zero units, total fixed cost can still be measured, but per-unit divisions are undefined.

To estimate a mixed bill from activity records, use the high-low method and its outlier checks. For the next calculation, follow the contribution-margin method and break-even formulas for units and sales dollars. Keep this page as the cost-classification reference rather than treating all four methods as interchangeable.

The direct answer

A fixed cost remains constant in total for a period, provided you stay within a normal operating range. If your shop sells 100 or 200 items this month, its monthly rent may still be $2,000. Other examples can include a basic insurance premium, a salaried office manager, accounting software, and a business license fee.

A variable cost changes in total as activity changes. If you make twice as many products, you generally buy more materials. If you serve more customers, you may use more ingredients, disposable supplies, shipping materials, or transaction-based labor. A cost that is $4 per unit creates $400 of total cost at 100 units and $800 at 200 units.

Use this basic structure:

  • Total fixed costs: costs that do not change in total with short-term volume.
  • Variable cost per unit: the activity-dependent cost for one defined unit, order, job or other driver, including applicable indirect variable costs.
  • Contribution margin per unit: selling price minus variable cost per unit.
  • Operating profit: total sales minus total variable costs minus total fixed costs.

For example, if you charge $30 for a service and spend $12 on supplies and payment-related costs, your contribution margin is $18 per service. If monthly fixed costs are $1,800, you need 100 services to cover that fixed-cost base because $1,800 ÷ $18 = 100. Sales above that point can contribute to operating profit, assuming the cost assumptions remain accurate.

What changes the answer

The time period matters. Rent is usually fixed month to month. Over several years, a lease may renew at a higher amount. State the time frame for your analysis.

The activity range matters. A small bakery may use its existing oven for 500 items a week. If demand reaches 1,000 items, it may need another oven or an extra shift. The original equipment cost behaves like a fixed cost within the first range, then the business takes a step up to a higher fixed-cost level.

Some costs are mixed. A phone plan can include a fixed monthly charge plus usage fees. A delivery arrangement can include a base fee plus a per-mile charge. Separate the base and usage portions when you can. If you cannot separate them precisely, make a reasonable estimate and label it as an assumption.

The unit must be clear. For a house cleaner, the unit might be one cleaning job. For a restaurant, it might be one meal, one order, or one cover. For a subscription business, a monthly subscriber may be the useful unit. Choose a unit that matches how you price and serve customers.

Timing is not the same as behavior. An annual insurance bill can create a large cash payment in one month, but the underlying expense may cover twelve months. Pricing policies can change variable cost. A discount may lower your revenue per unit without lowering ingredients, labor, or fulfillment costs. Free shipping may turn a cost you normally pass to the customer into a variable cost you absorb. Review the actual offer, not only the standard price.

Worked examples: Fixed Costs vs Variable Costs (With Examples)

These are independent fictional USD illustrations, each limited to its stated scope. Their prices are not current market-rate claims.

Scenario 1: House cleaning service

You charge $160 for a standard cleaning. Supplies cost $10 per job, payment processing averages $5 per job, and you pay a cleaner $85 per completed job. The variable cost per job is therefore $100:

$10 + $5 + $85 = $100

The contribution margin is $60 per job:

$160 - $100 = $60

Your monthly fixed costs are $2,400. They include insurance, scheduling software, phone service, storage, and a regular administrative wage. The break-even volume is:

$2,400 ÷ $60 = 40 jobs

At 40 jobs, revenue is $6,400 and variable costs are $4,000. The remaining $2,400 covers fixed costs, so operating profit is $0. At 45 jobs, revenue is $7,200 and variable costs are $4,500. After fixed costs, operating profit is $300:

$7,200 - $4,500 - $2,400 = $300

That calculation also shows why a price increase should be tested against demand. An extra $10 per job would increase contribution margin if job volume and variable cost stayed the same, but the result changes if the higher price reduces bookings. For related pricing decisions, see margin and markup.

Scenario 2: Small restaurant menu item

A restaurant sells a bowl for $14. Ingredients cost $4.20, the disposable container costs $0.60 for takeout orders, and a per-order fee averages $0.40. For a takeout bowl, variable cost is $5.20:

$4.20 + $0.60 + $0.40 = $5.20

The contribution margin is $8.80:

$14.00 - $5.20 = $8.80

Suppose monthly fixed costs allocated to the restaurant operation are $17,600. This includes rent, core salaried labor, insurance, and recurring systems. The number of bowls needed to cover that amount, if the bowl were the only item analyzed, is 2,000:

$17,600 ÷ $8.80 = 2,000 bowls

At 2,300 bowls, sales are $32,200. Variable costs are $11,960, calculated as 2,300 × $5.20. Operating profit after the stated fixed costs is $2,640:

$32,200 - $11,960 - $17,600 = $2,640

Scenario 3: Handmade product sold online

You sell a candle for $28. Wax and fragrance cost $6.50, the jar and label cost $3.50, packaging costs $2, and average payment and marketplace fees are $2.80. Total variable cost is $14.80:

$6.50 + $3.50 + $2.00 + $2.80 = $14.80

Contribution margin is $13.20 per candle:

$28.00 - $14.80 = $13.20

Monthly fixed costs are $1,584 for design software, insurance, a small studio, and baseline marketing subscriptions. Break-even volume is 120 candles:

$1,584 ÷ $13.20 = 120 candles

If you sell 150 candles, revenue is $4,200 and variable cost is $2,220. Operating profit is $396 after fixed costs:

$4,200 - $2,220 - $1,584 = $396

Four questions before classifying an expense

  1. Which period and activity? Materials follow production or consumption; merchant fees follow processed sales. Purchased stock, units produced and units sold can belong to different periods.
  2. What is payable at zero activity? Separate the lease, base fee, minimum purchase or guaranteed shift from usage charges.
  3. What changes at the next threshold? A new shift, overtime rate or all-units rebate requires its own cost schedule.
  4. Does the split reconcile to the bill? Fixed component + usage rate × matching activity must reproduce the included total. Keep invoice, quantity, contract and assumption together; count every amount once.

Behavior and traceability are different: directly attributable labor can be fixed when guaranteed, while shared supplies can vary with activity. Whether a fixed cost is avoidable depends on the decision and commitment period. The make-or-buy guide explains avoidable costs; an allocated fixed amount is not automatically an incremental cash saving.

Classify common expenses by the actual arrangement

Variable cost per activity unit = the selected total variable cost ÷ its matching activity. For inspection work, divide by comparable inspections; for delivery, mileage may be the driver. A variable-cost diagram shows the selected pool rising with activity; a mixed-cost line starts above zero because it includes a fixed component. Rebuild the model outside its relevant range. Use flexible budgeting to separate changed activity from spending differences without scaling every cost as variable.

How to run your own numbers

Start with one period, such as one month, and one unit of activity. A job, order, meal, or product is usually easier to analyze than a vague “customer.” Write down the price you actually collect, after routine discounts, rather than the list price.

Use the MyBreakeven calculator to test your assumptions.

Next, list every cost that increases when you deliver one more unit. Include materials, packaging, per-order fees, shipping you pay, commissions, and labor that is paid per job or hour of production. Divide the total by expected units to estimate variable cost per unit. Keep a note beside each estimate so you can replace it with actual results later.

Then total the costs that remain for the period even if you sell nothing. Include recurring rent, baseline payroll, insurance, subscriptions, licenses, and planned overhead. Do not count the same cost in both lists.

Use these formulas:

Contribution margin per unit = selling price per unit - variable cost per unit

Break-even units = total fixed costs ÷ contribution margin per unit

Operating profit = (units sold × contribution margin per unit) - total fixed costs

How to calculate variable cost per unit from your own jobs

For a service business, begin with completed jobs from one consistent period. Imagine a cleaning team delivered 80 standard visits last month. Supplies consumed on those visits cost an illustrative $640, payment fees were $240, and labor paid specifically to complete the visits was $5,600. These costs total $6,480. Divide by the 80 completed visits: $6,480 ÷ 80 = $81 variable cost per visit. At a collected price of $145 per visit, each job contributes $145 − $81 = $64 before monthly fixed costs.

That holds only while the job mix, collected price, per-job cost and available staff remain close to the assumptions. These are fictional example numbers, not typical US cleaning prices.

If a phone plan has a $95 base charge plus $0.30 for each booking, put the $95 in the period's fixed costs and $0.30 in cost per booking. A full $119 bill for 80 bookings is not $119 of variable cost; allocating the fixed base to every booking and also entering $95 as fixed would count it twice. If you run out of crew capacity at 50 visits and must pay a new guaranteed shift, calculate a second range with that added fixed or step cost instead of projecting the original $64 contribution indefinitely. Common mistakes

Calling every recurring cost fixed. A monthly bill may contain a usage component. Separate the base charge from the amount that grows with activity.

Ignoring labor that follows sales. If you pay someone per job, per item, or per hour worked, that labor belongs in the variable-cost calculation for the relevant decision. Otherwise, your contribution margin will look too high.

Using revenue instead of contribution margin. Revenue does not show what remains after fulfilling an order. Break-even volume based only on price will understate the sales needed.

Mixing cash timing with cost behavior. An annual renewal is not automatically a variable cost because cash leaves the bank once a year. Spread the expense for operating analysis while separately planning the cash payment.

Forgetting discounts, refunds, and waste. Your real selling price may be lower than the advertised price. Your real material usage may be higher than the recipe or bill of materials. Use observed averages when possible.

Rounding too early. Keep cents through the contribution-margin calculation. Round the final break-even unit target up because partial units do not cover a real sales target.

Separate average cost from variable cost and step costs

Average total cost per job changes when fixed costs are spread over a different number of jobs. In a separate illustration with $3,200 monthly fixed costs and $81 variable cost per job, 40 jobs cost $3,200 + 40 × $81 = $6,440, averaging $161 each. At 80 jobs, total cost is $9,680, averaging $121 each. Variable cost remains $81 within the assumed operating range.

Do not enter the $121 average as variable cost while also entering $3,200 fixed costs: that would count the fixed allocation twice. Nor should the declining average be used to promise that every additional job becomes cheaper.

Now suppose exceeding 60 jobs requires an extra $800 monthly commitment. At 70 jobs, fixed costs become $4,000 and total cost is $4,000 + 70 × $81 = $9,670. At a $145 price, revenue is $10,150 and the modeled surplus is $480. Ignoring the step would overstate that surplus by $800.

Write down the capacity threshold, commitment duration and which charges apply to existing as well as new jobs. A subscription upgrade that changes the fee on every order needs a whole-period recalculation, not just a fee applied to the extra orders.

At 60 visits: $8,700 − $4,860 − $3,200 = $640. At 61: $8,845 − $4,941 − $4,000 = −$96. One extra visit adds $64 contribution but triggers $800 of fixed cost, reducing the remainder by $736. The original $3,200 includes an owner compensation allocation. Check a new staffing commitment’s duration and reversibility before accepting additional work. The CVP guide covers the wider profit method; this example shows why cost classification comes first.

Estimate mixed costs without double-counting

A fixed monthly vehicle commitment plus usage-dependent running costs is a mixed cost. If comparable observations show $1,640 at 80 equivalent visits and $2,440 at 280, the two-point estimate is ($2,440 − $1,640) ÷ (280 − 80) = $4 per visit; its monthly fixed component is $1,320. Check both observations: $1,320 + $4 × 80 = $1,640, and $1,320 + $4 × 280 = $2,440. At 200 equivalent visits the estimate is $2,120, averaging $10.60 per visit; that includes the fixed allocation and is not the $4 variable rate. Select the high and low observations by activity, not cost, and inspect all intermediate records. The high-low method calculator and six-month example shows why a high repair bill can distort a model.

Cost behavior and traceability are different classifications: a cost can be directly attributable to a service while remaining fixed for the month, or indirect yet variable with activity. State the cost object and relevant range. After splitting a mixed cost, enter its fixed component once in overhead and variable component once per activity unit; do not add the original total again.

Use the axes before interpreting a curve. In this independent fictional period, total fixed cost is $2,000, total variable cost is $20 × activity and a separate mixed-cost example is $1,000 + $10 × activity. The fixed line is horizontal on a total-cost chart; it is not horizontal on a cost-per-unit chart. These are three separate cost examples, not three components to add together.

A capacity step can invalidate the old line

Suppose a separate staffing arrangement costs $2,000 through 100 jobs and requires a second $2,000 shift for 101–200 jobs. The fixed commitment is $2,000 at 100 jobs and $4,000 at 101. It is a step schedule, not the horizontal $2,000 assumption used in the chart. Review the contract and practical capacity; do not extend a line beyond its relevant range.

Accounting function is a separate dimension. An expense may be selling OPEX and variable, or administrative OPEX and fixed; production costs can also contain fixed and variable elements. The operating-expense guide owns classification against COGS, while the operating-margin calculator subtracts compatible statement totals. Do not transfer every OPEX line into a variable-cost field merely because it is an operating expense.

Compare a higher fixed commitment with a higher per-order charge

Consider two independent fictional fulfillment arrangements for identical service quality and scope. Option A costs $4,800 a month plus $20 per order; option B costs $1,200 plus $50 per order. They have equal modeled total cost at ($4,800 − $1,200) ÷ ($50 − $20) = 120 orders: each costs $7,200. At 80 orders A costs $6,400 and B $5,200; at 160 orders A costs $8,000 and B $9,200.

This is a cost-indifference point, not the business’s sales break-even point. It excludes selling price, financing, switching costs, capacity and contract minimums beyond those stated. Check those conditions before selecting an arrangement. The make-or-buy decision guide covers avoidable costs and capacity; the CVP guide shows how selling price and contribution change the profit calculation.

Method references and example boundaries

Reviewed November 13, 2026. The cases are independently constructed illustrations; the sources are not providers of these business prices.

Use compatible costs and activity for the same period. A linear model assumes stable selling price, variable rates and sales mix within its relevant range. Zero or negative contribution cannot fund positive fixed commitments through extra volume. Keep financing principal, equipment cash purchases and payment dates in a separate cash plan; a positive modeled remainder does not establish sufficient bank cash. Review working capital and asset quality when funding commitments.

Distinguish incremental tiers from an all-units price change

A lower rate above a threshold can mean two different contracts. In this fictional 0–200-order operating range, both arrangements have a $600 fixed monthly commitment. Contract A charges $8 for each of the first 100 orders, then $6 only for additional orders. Contract B charges $8 per order through 100; if qualifying monthly volume exceeds 100, its $6 rate applies to every order in that month. Assume identical scope and no other charges.

For contract A, total cost is 600 + 8 × MIN(Q,100) + 6 × MAX(Q − 100,0). For contract B it is 600 + IF(Q ≤ 100,8 × Q,6 × Q). These spreadsheet-style expressions require nonnegative whole Q within the stated range. The $600 remains fixed; the usage charge follows the applicable piecewise schedule.

At the 101st order, A’s total bill rises by $6. B’s modeled bill falls by $194 because the prior 100 orders also receive the $2 reduction: $6 for the extra order minus $200 of repricing. Do not generalize that result to a real supplier without verifying eligibility, minimum commitments, credits and the period when the rebate is earned. An annual purchasing rebate is not automatically available in a monthly cost model.

A single $6 or $8 rate cannot describe every point in both contracts. Nor is total bill divided by orders the variable rate: it includes the $600 fixed allocation. Keep the schedule, driver and activity range in the input record. For inventory, distinguish purchased units from consumed or sold units before assigning a period expense. The high-low estimation guide does not turn a known tier schedule into one reliable straight line; the transaction-fee allocation example shows the parallel need to define the selling unit.

faq.q: What is the variable cost per unit formula?
faq.a: Add the costs that increase when you deliver the units in a comparable period, then divide by the number of completed units. Check that each expense is included once and the units share a comparable scope.

faq.q: Is an hourly wage always a variable cost?
faq.a: Job-paid production time often changes with completed work, but a guaranteed shift may remain payable even if bookings fall. Model the actual pay arrangement and staffing range rather than assuming all labor behaves the same way.

faq.q: Can an annual payment be a fixed cost?
faq.a: Yes. Fixed and variable describe cost behavior as activity changes, not the date cash leaves the account. Plan the annual cash payment separately from the operating analysis.

faq.q: What if one job takes twice as long as another?
faq.a: Use job types or a weighted mix rather than one average across unlike services. A deep clean and a standard maintenance visit may need separate per-job labor and price assumptions.

faq.q: Are payment-processing fees fixed or variable?
faq.a: A per-transaction or percentage fee varies with the matching sales activity. A monthly account charge or minimum can add a fixed component. Separate the contract’s base and usage amounts without counting either twice.

faq.q: Can a cost be partly fixed and partly variable?
faq.a: Yes. A base subscription plus a per-order charge is a simple example. Enter the base in monthly commitments and the incremental charge in sale-dependent cost, each counted once.

faq.q: How do you calculate total fixed cost?
faq.a: Subtract total variable cost from total cost for the same period and scope. If the variable rate is independently known, total fixed cost equals total cost minus variable cost per unit multiplied by units. In this guide, $9,680 minus $81 times 80 visits equals $3,200.

faq.q: Does a lower tiered rate apply to all units or only extra units?
faq.a: The contract determines that. An incremental tier changes the charge only for units in that tier. An all-units arrangement can reprice every qualifying unit when a threshold is met. Record the applicable range and rebate timing before using either rate in a contribution calculation.

faq.q: Does fixed cost per unit stay constant?
faq.a: No. The total can stay fixed within a stated range while its allocation per unit changes. A $3,200 fixed cost spread over 80 visits is $40 per visit; over 40 it is $80. At zero visits, the per-visit allocation is undefined.

faq.q: Can extra sales create a loss after a capacity step?
faq.a: Yes. In the stated example, 60 visits leave $640. The 61st adds $64 contribution but triggers $800 extra monthly commitments, leaving a $96 shortfall. The new 61–100-visit range requires 63 whole visits to cover $4,000 of included fixed costs.

targets.html:
If sales rise 10%, profit might rise much more than 10%. It might also fall quickly when demand softens. Operating leverage describes that sensitivity when your fixed costs stay in place while sales volume changes. The calculation is most useful beside a break-even point and an actual staffing plan. Near break-even, an impressive leverage number can be a warning rather than a growth forecast.

Calculate it from a real cost structure

Take a fictional owner-operated service business completing 120 comparable jobs in a four-week planning month. Each job collects $200 and uses $80 of paid direct labor, supplies, travel and processing fees. Contribution is $120 per job. Monthly fixed operating costs, including the owner's planned base salary, are $12,000. These are example inputs, not US price or wage averages.

Break-even is $12,000 ÷ $120 = 100 jobs. That twenty-job gap between current volume and break-even explains why a moderate change matters. The break-even formula guide derives the volume threshold; this article asks what happens to profit when volume moves around the current 120 jobs. OpenStax covers the underlying operating-leverage and margin-of-safety calculation.

See what a 10% sales change really does

Ten percent of 120 jobs is 12 jobs. If those jobs have the same $120 contribution and require no new fixed resources, a move to 132 jobs adds 12 × $120 = $1,440 operating profit. Profit becomes $3,840, a 60% rise from $2,400. At 108 jobs, contribution falls by $1,440 and profit becomes $960, a 60% fall. That is the meaning of DOL 6 at the 120-job starting point: roughly 6 × 10% = 60% sensitivity to a small percentage volume change in the same operating range.

Completed jobs Sales Contribution Operating profit Change from 120-job profit
90 $18,000 $10,800 −$1,200 Below break-even
100 $20,000 $12,000 $0 Break-even
108 $21,600 $12,960 $960 −60%
120 $24,000 $14,400 $2,400 Starting point
132 $26,400 $15,840 $3,840 +60%
150 $30,000 $18,000 $6,000 Different starting DOL

Do not carry “six times” to every volume. At 150 jobs the same model has DOL = $18,000 ÷ $6,000 = 3. At exactly 100 jobs, operating profit is zero and division by zero makes DOL undefined. Below break-even, a negative ratio is not a useful promise of favorable growth. Use the contribution and profit dollars directly for stress tests when profit is tiny or negative.

Why fixed costs and capacity change the interpretation

An owner may hire a salaried manager to free time for sales. Suppose that adds $3,000 monthly fixed cost with no immediate change in job economics. Fixed costs become $15,000. At 120 jobs, contribution is still $14,400 and the business now loses $600. New break-even is $15,000 ÷ $120 = 125 jobs. If that hire enables 150 completed jobs, profit becomes $18,000 − $15,000 = $3,000. The hiring decision can work, but its merit depends on actual capacity, leads, transition time and cash to cover the early shortfall, not on a simple DOL comparison.

There is a second side. If the owner instead pays a contractor per completed job, variable cost may rise while fixed cost stays lower. At the same selling price, that lowers contribution per job but may avoid a guaranteed salary during slow months. Neither arrangement is universally better. Model likely volume and service quality under each staffing plan. Our fixed-versus-variable costs guide helps classify the actual pay arrangement rather than the employee's job title.

The DOL formula assumes the relevant range stays stable. Overtime premiums, a second vehicle, new software seats or a larger workshop can change costs at particular volumes. If 132 jobs require another guaranteed shift, the neat $3,840 profit calculation overstates the result by that shift's additional fixed cost. Put a capacity step in the scenario instead of stretching one straight line beyond the hours you can sell.

Compare three decisions at the right volume

Protect the base: At 120 jobs, a 10% loss of work cuts profit from $2,400 to $960. If one customer accounts for 12 jobs, concentration deserves attention even though the current month is profitable. The margin of safety guide expresses that risk as the unit and sales gap from break-even.

Raise the price: If every job collects $210 with the same $80 variable cost and demand genuinely stays at 120, contribution becomes $130 per job. Monthly profit is 120 × $130 − $12,000 = $3,600. DOL at that new starting point is $15,600 ÷ $3,600 = 4.33, rounded. Price changes can affect demand; run a lower-volume case before treating all $1,200 of modeled improvement as certain.

Add capacity: A $3,000 fixed manager cost needs at least 25 extra $120-contribution jobs to cover itself, assuming no other changes. From 120 to 145 jobs, the incremental contribution is 25 × $120 = $3,000. New profit at 145 is 145 × $120 − $15,000 = $2,400, the same as the old 120-job profit. The manager has paid for the added cost but has not yet improved operating profit. This comparison is more decision-ready than quoting a DOL number in isolation.

How to run your own numbers

In the MyBreakeven general calculator, enter an average collected price, per-job costs and monthly fixed costs, then compare feasible volumes above and below break-even. Calculate contribution ÷ operating profit at your current positive-profit volume, and add any staffing or space step separately. The site supports other currencies; the US-dollar numbers are only the worked example.

Common mistakes

Dividing revenue by profit. DOL uses contribution after variable costs in the numerator. Revenue includes dollars needed to deliver the work.

Using DOL at exactly break-even. Operating profit is zero there, so the ratio is undefined. Show the dollar loss or gain for a concrete volume change.

Applying the current ratio to a big expansion. DOL changes with volume, and fixed or variable costs may step up when capacity changes. Recompute the income statement.

Classifying every worker as fixed. Job-paid crew time often varies by job; a guaranteed shift may act as a fixed or step cost within the relevant range.

Assuming a price increase preserves demand. A higher contribution per job helps only for jobs you can sell and deliver. Test the volume response rather than asserting one.

Calling operating profit cash. Receivables, equipment purchases, tax and debt payments can make cash timing different from the modeled operating result.

Operating leverage changes when contribution and fixed costs move

Operating leverage describes how a change in sales affects operating profit under a stated cost structure. A simple degree-of-operating-leverage calculation divides contribution by operating profit when the definitions are consistent and profit is positive. Suppose contribution is $10,000 and fixed operating costs are $8,000. Operating profit is $2,000 and the ratio is five.

Under unchanged price, mix, unit costs and fixed costs, a 10% sales increase would raise contribution to $11,000 and operating profit to $3,000, a 50% increase. A 10% decline would leave $9,000 contribution and $1,000 profit. These are conditional arithmetic scenarios, not forecasts.

Near zero profit the ratio becomes unstable, and at zero it is undefined. Do not present a very large ratio as a growth promise. Step costs, capacity constraints, discounts and changing sales mix can break the simplified relationship. Keep owner-pay treatment consistent when comparing this accounting-style measure with a calculator's separately modeled income target.

FAQs

What does an operating leverage ratio of 6 mean?

At the specific starting volume and cost structure, a small percentage sales-volume change is associated with about six times that percentage change in operating profit. In the example, 10% more jobs increases profit by 60%. The ratio changes when volume or costs change.

Is high operating leverage good or bad?

It creates more profit sensitivity in both directions under stable costs. It may help when demand rises and capacity is available, and hurt when revenue falls while fixed bills remain. Judge it against your demand variability and cash buffer.

Can I calculate DOL when the business loses money?

The quotient can be negative, but the familiar percentage-change interpretation becomes misleading near or below zero profit. Show contribution, fixed costs, break-even volume and a few specific sales scenarios instead.

Why does operating leverage fall as sales rise?

If fixed costs and per-unit contribution hold, operating profit grows after fixed costs are covered. The contribution-to-profit ratio shrinks as profit grows. In the example it falls from 6 at 120 jobs to 3 at 150 jobs.

Does hiring a manager automatically raise operating leverage?

It increases fixed cost in this example, which can increase sensitivity if the business remains profitable, but may first create a loss. Assess the additional jobs or higher price the hire makes possible and include the time needed to reach them.

What if the business sells several services?

Use a documented mix of service prices and variable costs to find total contribution for the period. Recalculate when the mix shifts. One premium job's margin should not stand in for every appointment.

Why is operating leverage unreliable near break-even?

The profit denominator is very small or zero. Small assumption changes can produce a large or undefined ratio. Use explicit sales and cost scenarios instead of treating that ratio as a reliable prediction.

What to remember

  • DOL = contribution ÷ positive operating profit at a stated volume.
  • At 120 example jobs, a 10% volume change moves profit about 60% within the unchanged cost range.
  • Near break-even the ratio becomes unstable; use dollar scenarios.
  • Check staffing steps, demand and cash before acting on leverage.

Find related calculations in the MyBreakeven guide library.

Check volume before interpreting sensitivity

Test required sales and available capacity with your own price, variable costs and monthly commitments. That planner does not calculate operating leverage; use this guide for the ratio and its positive-operating-profit boundary. More required volume is not evidence that demand exists. Find the related contribution and margin-of-safety guides for the cost definitions and sales cushion.

Document fixed depreciation before interpreting sensitivity

When the model includes depreciation as fixed operating expense, its sensitivity describes that defined operating-profit basis. The straight-line schedule documents the period allocation; the accumulated depreciation rollforward explains the asset balance. Neither allocation is a current-period equipment cash payment. Keep the original leverage formula and cost classification consistent, and prepare a separate cash sensitivity if that is the decision. A near-zero operating-profit denominator can make the leverage ratio unstable without describing a reliable forecast.

Operating leverage formula: contribution divided by operating profit

Degree of operating leverage (DOL) = total contribution margin ÷ operating profit at a stated starting sales level. For the positive-profit interpretation used here, contribution is sales less variable costs, and operating profit is contribution less fixed operating costs.

The fictional USD month below has $14,400 contribution and $2,400 operating profit: DOL = 6. With unchanged price, variable cost per unit, sales mix and fixed costs inside the same operating range, a 10% volume change produces a 60% operating-profit change from that starting point. It does not predict sales or cash.

At zero operating profit the ratio is undefined. At a loss, do not interpret a negative ratio as the same positive-profit sensitivity measure; near zero profit, small input changes can make the ratio unstable. Review the full assumptions and capacity limits.

Variable costs 120 × $80 $9,600
Contribution $24,000 − $9,600 $14,400
Fixed operating costs Assumed monthly budget $12,000
Operating profit before tax and financing $14,400 − $12,000 $2,400

Choose the restaurant budgeting resource for your task

This restaurant budget template pairs an editable Excel workbook with a monthly planning example. Use it to budget sales, food costs, loaded payroll and recurring overhead, then compare actual results with your original plan.

A restaurant budget should tell you how many sales must arrive this month and what remains after food, labor, occupancy and owner pay. Start with orders or covers and an average check, then budget costs on the same monthly basis. Compare actual results with that plan as the month progresses. A lease budget written only as percentages cannot tell you whether Tuesday service will pay for a guaranteed shift.

Quick answer: Forecast monthly orders and average check, subtract variable food and transaction costs, then subtract the costs due even when orders are slow. For example, 2,000 orders at $25 bring $50,000 sales; at $9 variable cost each, contribution is $32,000. With $27,000 fixed costs, the example leaves $5,000 modeled remainder after the included owner allocation. Make your own budget using quoted costs.

Verified restaurant cost data for your budget

Reviewed November 13, 2026. The National Restaurant Association’s 2025 Restaurant Operations Data Abstract reports 2024 operating data from more than 900 U.S. restaurants. These are segment-specific survey medians, not 2026 supplier quotes, forecasts or prescribed targets.

2024 U.S. restaurant survey medians, reported in 2025
MeasureFullserviceLimited-service
Food and nonalcoholic beverage costs / sales32.0%32.4%
Income before taxes / sales2.8%4.0%

Sources: National Restaurant Association food-cost findings, September 10, 2025, and profitability findings, August 20, 2025. The Association cautions that these ratios are not individual restaurant standards or goals.

Compare account definitions, service type and sales mix before judging a difference. Separate medians do not form a single restaurant income statement. Our fictional workbook’s $11,800 remainder on $60,000 sales (19.67%) is not an industry net-margin claim: its cost scope and owner-pay treatment differ. Build your own budget from current inventory, recipes, payroll schedules, contracts and channel statements.

How to budget a restaurant in five steps

  1. Choose the calendar month or accounting period, then forecast orders or covers by daypart and channel. Multiply each by the expected average check.
  2. Use inventory records for food and beverage cost, and record channel-dependent fees and packaging separately.
  3. Build paid hours by role, including employer costs. Separate guaranteed shifts from hours added for incremental orders.
  4. Add occupancy and other recurring commitments, counting owner compensation once. Keep equipment, deposits and financing payments in a separate cash schedule.
  5. Save the original budget. Compare actual results each week, explain the largest dollar variances, and update a separate forecast.

The workbook example below follows its stated simplified cost boundary. Add any missing channel costs before using it as your own break-even model. A target percentage cannot replace the minimum staffing and payments your operation actually needs.

The monthly restaurant budget, line by line

Start with food and beverage revenue separately. Estimate covers by daypart, open days and average spend, not a single hopeful annual growth rate. Then enter food and beverage cost of goods sold (COGS), guaranteed payroll including employer costs, rent, utilities, marketing, owner pay and other fixed charges. Put opening equipment and deposits in a cash schedule; they are not the same as this month's cost of serving a meal. The OpenStax break-even guide explains why fixed and variable costs need separate treatment for break-even.

A simple test uses 2,000 orders at $25 average spend: sales are $50,000. Ingredients, packaging and payment fees of $9 an order total $18,000, leaving $32,000 contribution. Assume rent, guaranteed labor, insurance, owner pay and other fixed costs total $27,000. The modeled remainder after the included owner allocation is $5,000; this is not after-tax net income or bank cash. Required orders to cover those fixed costs are $27,000 ÷ ($25 − $9), rounded up to 1,688 orders. At 26 open days, that is about 65 orders daily. Compare the required volume with your actual service capacity.

Restaurant budget template for Excel: read the example first

The editable sheet below uses a separate illustrative month from the $50,000 sales example above. Its budget is $45,000 food sales plus $15,000 beverage sales. Food and beverage cost of goods sold total $18,000. The committed expense lines total $30,200: $15,000 guaranteed payroll, $1,500 employer payroll costs, $4,000 owner compensation, $6,000 occupancy, $1,200 utilities, $800 marketing and $1,700 other fixed costs. Owner compensation is included once.

Illustrative monthly restaurant budget and actual results in USD
LineBudgetActualActual less budget
Food sales$45,000$42,000−$3,000
Beverage sales$15,000$15,000$0
Total sales$60,000$57,000−$3,000
Food and beverage COGS$18,000$18,700+$700
Sales less COGS$42,000$38,300−$3,700
Committed expense lines including owner compensation$30,200$31,100+$900
Modeled remainder after owner allocation$11,800$7,200−$4,600

Reconcile the change: $3,000 less sales, $700 more COGS and $900 more committed expenses reduce the modeled remainder by $4,600. A positive expense variance means actual spending exceeded the budget; it is not automatically a favorable result. Keep the original budget so you can explain each difference before revising the forecast.

The sheet's simplified break-even calculation treats COGS as its only variable cost and the listed recurring expenses as committed. Budget contribution is $42,000 ÷ $60,000 = 70%, giving $30,200 ÷ 0.70 = $43,142.86 break-even sales. Actual contribution is $38,300 ÷ $57,000 = 67.19% when displayed to two decimals; using the unrounded ratio gives $46,284.60 break-even sales. Payment fees, delivery commissions and volume-dependent labor need separate treatment if they apply to your business. Include each cost once in a consistent category, and adapt the sheet or use a model that includes those costs before treating its result as your own threshold.

This operating budget does not show bank cash, tax liabilities, debt principal or equipment payments. The loaded restaurant labor guide helps reconcile wages and employer costs with these payroll lines; keep opening purchases and payment timing in a separate cash schedule.

When the workbook cannot report a break-even threshold

The contribution calculation requires positive sales. If sales are zero, the workbook shows No sales; if sales less COGS is zero or negative, it shows No positive contribution instead of a zero or negative break-even target. Adding volume at that contribution does not fund positive monthly commitments. Complete inputs means a required amount is blank or nonnumeric, while Check inputs identifies a negative entered amount. Enter a genuine zero explicitly. The break-even variance is Not comparable unless both columns have numeric thresholds. A valid zero threshold is possible when all committed costs are explicitly zero and contribution is positive.

These checks do not validate demand or add omitted costs. The workbook remains a simplified operating model; use a dated cash forecast for payment timing and check service capacity separately.

Use a budget that changes when the month changes

Your monthly budget is the original target. Update a rolling forecast when bookings, sales mix, staff hours or ingredient invoices change; keep the original target to measure the difference. A $3,000 favorable sales variance may still leave you behind if a delivery channel carries $2,000 extra commissions. Separate the variance in sales volume from the variance in average ticket.

Include payroll taxes and employer insurance in labor, and split minimum scheduled hours from extra hours needed for a busy service. Treat fixed rent and software differently from per-order processing fees. If your supplier prices rise, adjust the cost per plate rather than multiplying the entire restaurant's expenses by the same inflation number. The budget is only useful when its expense categories match invoices and the owner can update it each week.

Three budget outcomes from the same dining room

Base case: 2,000 orders × $25 = $50,000 sales. Variable cost is 2,000 × $9 = $18,000. Contribution is $32,000; less $27,000 fixed costs leaves $5,000.

Slow month: 1,600 orders at the same ticket give $40,000 sales. Variable cost is $14,400, leaving $25,600 contribution. With the same guaranteed shifts and rent, the restaurant loses $1,400. Changing the order count alone changes the answer; copying last month's percentage profit would hide that loss.

Discounted delivery mix: 2,200 orders at an average $23 ticket give $50,600 sales. If packaging, commissions and food raise blended variable cost to $11 per order, contribution is $26,400 and the business loses $600 after fixed costs. Higher order count did not repair the weaker contribution. Check channel mix before praising a sales increase.

Explain the $4,600 shortfall with a flexible comparison

This uses the same monthly workbook example, not a new restaurant dataset. Original COGS is $18,000 ÷ $60,000 = 30% of sales. Applied to $57,000 actual sales, the allowance is $17,100. Holding $30,200 commitments constant gives a flexible comparison of $9,700. This is a manual analysis; no additional workbook tab is claimed.

Original budget, flexed comparison and actual: illustrative USD
LineOriginal budgetFlexed to actual salesActual
Net sales$60,000$57,000$57,000
Food and beverage COGS$18,000$17,100$18,700
Commitments including owner allocation$30,200$30,200$31,100
Modeled remainder$11,800$9,700$7,200
  1. Lower-sales effect: −$2,100. ($57,000 − $60,000) × 70% budget contribution margin.
  2. COGS above flexed allowance: −$1,600. $17,100 allowed − $18,700 actual.
  3. Additional commitments: −$900. $30,200 budget − $31,100 actual.

Check: −$2,100 − $1,600 − $900 = −$4,600; $11,800 − $4,600 = $7,200. The static COGS variance is only $700, but COGS is $1,600 above the sales-adjusted allowance. Investigate inventory usage, prices, waste and menu mix before cutting an unrelated expense.

This revenue-based flex assumes stable prices, mix and cost behavior within the modeled range. Without covers, quantities and realized prices, the $2,100 cannot be attributed solely to fewer guests. Flex recipes and staffing to actual activity by channel for a real diagnosis. OpenStax explains the activity-based flexible-budget principle.

Calculate budget inputs from source records

These independent USD illustrations explain individual input lines; do not add them again to totals already entered. Use net sales after discounts and refunds, excluding sales tax collected for remittance. A cover is one guest; an order can include several guests. Match the unit to the average check.

Illustrative calculations and supporting records
InputExact calculationCheck against
Net sales2,000 orders × $25 = $50,000POS net sales, refunds and channel totals
Inventory-based COGS$6,000 opening inventory + $19,000 net purchases − $6,300 closing inventory = $18,700Same-period counts, valuations, transfers and adjustments
Loaded labor600 paid hours × $20 + $1,200 employer costs = $13,200Roster and payroll; the assumed 10% burden is not a statutory rate
Delivery commission$10,000 commissionable sales × assumed 25% = $2,500Contract and settlement statement; charging bases differ
Prime cost percentage($18,700 COGS + $13,200 loaded labor) ÷ $57,000 net sales = 55.96%Consistent period and sales denominator; include all applicable labor once

Add separate delivery commission once if it is absent from entered costs. Do not both net it out of revenue and subtract it again. Split guaranteed staffing from incremental hours before calculating contribution; payroll is not automatically entirely fixed or entirely variable.

Check rounding, capacity and owner compensation

For the $50,000 quick example, contribution is $25 − $9 = $16 per order. The exact threshold is $27,000 ÷ $16 = 1,687.5 orders: 1,688 whole orders. The fractional daily average over 26 open days is 64.9038; a uniform whole-order target is 65 orders daily. That gives 1,690 monthly orders and a $40 remainder; 1,688 monthly orders leave $8. Check kitchen and seating capacity separately.

The $27,000 quick-example commitments and $30,200 monthly workbook commitments include owner compensation once. The result is a planning remainder after the stated owner allocation, not automatically accounting operating profit, withdrawable cash or after-tax net income. Salary, drawings and distributions have different treatment depending on entity structure. Keep drawings, debt principal, capital purchases and payment timing in a separate cash schedule.

The one-month workbook treats COGS as its only variable cost: its budget contribution margin is 70%. The separate annual workbook also includes packaging/delivery/fees. Its sample monthly base is $60,000 sales − $18,000 COGS − $1,800 variable fees = $40,200 contribution (67%). Less $30,200 commitments leaves $10,000; break-even is $45,074.63. Do not transfer a margin between files without reconciling included costs. Enter every actual input, including genuine zeros, before interpreting an annual workbook month.

Operating budget: original target, flexible comparison and cash plan

An operating budget estimates same-period revenue and operating expenses. An annual operating budget can be built from monthly sales drivers, expense behavior and seasonal schedules rather than spreading every line equally across twelve months. Keep the original approved target unchanged so the comparison remains auditable.

At month end, compare actual results with a budget flexed to actual activity using original rates. This distinguishes fewer orders from unfavorable ingredients or staffing costs. The operating-budget result is not the bank balance: equipment purchases, loan principal and collection/payment timing require a separate cash budget.

Connect the restaurant budget to its supporting schedules

A restaurant operating budget is part of a wider master budget. Keep the sales plan, purchasing and staffing needs, payment dates, equipment spending and financing connected. The service example in that guide is a simplified bridge; add inventory, unpaid bills, deposits and other restaurant-specific timing rather than copying its assumptions unchanged.

How to run your own numbers

Download the budget and replace the yellow sales and expense inputs with your own month. The example has budget and actual columns and shows the difference for each line. It is an operating model, so prepare a separate cash forecast for debt principal, equipment purchases and sales-tax remittances.

Use the editable restaurant monthly budget template. Replace the yellow sample inputs; its figures are illustrations, not benchmarks.

Enter your own average ticket, variable cost, monthly fixed costs, owner pay and operating capacity in the free restaurant break-even calculator. It is a planning model, not a forecast of customer demand.

Common budgeting mistakes

Using purchases as food cost. Inventory bought in the last week may not be used until next month; reconcile opening inventory, purchases and closing inventory. Ignoring owner hours. Profit improves on paper when the owner works a full schedule without a wage, even if that arrangement is unsustainable.

Changing the target when results disappoint. Keep budget and revised forecast side by side. Budgeting labor as a flat percentage. A two-person minimum shift costs money even when no one walks in. Mixing sales tax with revenue. Remitted tax is not operating sales; keep your accounting basis consistent.

Restaurant monthly expenses: reconcile before judging the variance

Use the same month and accounting boundary in both workbook columns. Keep the approved budget, collect actual records, then explain differences before changing next month’s forecast. This checklist supports the existing one-month file; it does not add automated imports or a twelve-month dashboard.

Monthly budget review: evidence and next decision
Line to reviewEvidence and action
Food and beverage salesReconcile net sales by channel and daypart. Separate fewer covers from a lower average check; do not include tax collected for another party as sales.
Food and beverage COGSReconcile beginning inventory + purchases − ending inventory. Investigate quantities, purchase prices and waste rather than treating every higher invoice as higher consumption.
Payroll and employer costsMatch paid hours, pay rates and employer charges to the period. Count owner compensation once and separate minimum shifts from additional hours.
Other recurring expensesCheck rent, utilities, subscriptions and invoice timing. Identify delivery commissions, payment fees and packaging before relying on the sheet’s simplified contribution ratio.
Cash commitments outside this resultSchedule deposits, equipment and debt principal in the cash forecast. A favorable operating variance does not establish that cash is available.

In the existing workbook example, the $4,600 unfavorable operating-result variance consists of $3,000 less sales, $700 more COGS and $900 more committed expenses. It identifies the dollar bridge; it does not prove that food waste or staff inefficiency caused the change. Compare actual activity with original rates using flexible budget and variance analysis before making that decision.

Download the restaurant monthly budget, retain a dated original for the period and record the explanation beside each material variance. Keep opening costs in the restaurant startup budget.

Diagnose a restaurant budget variance before cutting costs

Keep the original budget intact. Then ask three separate questions: did you serve the planned number of orders, did each order leave the planned contribution, and did monthly committed costs change? A lower food bill can simply mean fewer customers; it does not prove purchasing improved.

Independent USD example: a volume and cost bridge, not the downloadable workbook's default inputs
MeasureOriginal budgetActual month
Completed orders × net average check2,000 × $25 = $50,0001,800 × $25 = $45,000
Order-driven costs per order$9$10
Contribution before monthly costs$32,000$27,000
Committed monthly operating costs$27,000$27,500
Operating result in this stated scope$5,000−$500

The $5,500 deterioration reconciles exactly: 200 missing orders × $16 budget contribution = $3,200; $1 extra order-driven cost × 1,800 actual orders = $1,800; and $500 more monthly costs. The flexible comparison at actual volume would be 1,800 × $16 − $27,000 = $1,800. Actual performance is $2,300 below that comparison. This separates volume from cost changes without claiming a cause.

At the new $15 contribution, covering $27,500 needs 1,834 whole orders; recovering the original $5,000 operating result needs 2,167. Check staffing, service hours and demand before treating either number as an achievable plan. This example excludes separate owner compensation, tax, financing and any unentered items.

Match each budget line to a source record

  • Sales: reconcile POS net sales by channel and service period. Keep customer taxes, tips and marketplace settlements distinct from the restaurant's sales.
  • Ingredients used: reconcile opening stock plus purchases minus closing stock, with a consistent scope for transfers, credits and waste. Buying a month's stock is different from using it that month.
  • Labor: reconcile the roster, paid hours and employer costs. Keep committed staffing in monthly costs and genuinely additional order-driven labor in direct costs; do not count the same shift in both.
  • Delivery and payment fees: reconcile each channel's merchant statement. Do not add a second processing charge when the contracted fee already includes it.
  • Overhead and cash: compare bills with the reporting period, then separately schedule their payment dates. Equipment purchases, loan principal and owner drawings need a cash plan even when outside the operating result.

Investigate the largest dollar movement first, record its evidence and assign one action with a review date. For example, inspect portion and waste records before calling the $1 direct-cost increase supplier inflation. Keep the budget versus actual report for period review and the 13-week cash forecast for payment timing.

What to do after the first month

Compare budget with actual by food, beverages, labor and fixed categories. If food cost ran high, identify whether portions, purchase prices, waste or theft changed; do not assume the menu price is wrong. If sales fell, compare order counts by daypart and channel with what you expected. Use those observations to forecast the next month, then test whether the revised daily order target can actually be served.

  • Build sales from orders and average checks.
  • Keep guaranteed labor and per-sale costs distinct.
  • Compare actuals with the original budget before updating the forecast.
  • Maintain a separate cash schedule for opening and financing payments.

Build an annual restaurant budget from seasonal monthly plans

A restaurant annual budget should add twelve dated monthly plans rather than multiply its busiest month by twelve. Keep covers or completed orders, net average sale, food usage, loaded payroll and other commitments visible in each month. Use the same reporting scope when comparing a monthly restaurant budget example with actual results.

Independent fictional annual illustration, USD; not the workbook default
LineCalculationAnnual amount
Net salesJanuary 80,000 + February 90,000 + ten months at 100,0001,170,000
Food COGS35% of each month’s net sales409,500
Loaded payroll30,000 each month × 12360,000
Other included operating costs20,000 each month × 12240,000
Operating result1,170,000 − 409,500 − 360,000 − 240,000160,500

The modeled operating margin is 13.72%, rounded. January contributes only $2,000 under this scope: $80,000 less $28,000 food, $30,000 payroll and $20,000 other costs. An annual positive result therefore does not establish that every monthly payment date is funded. The example holds staffing and other monthly costs constant solely to isolate seasonality; test actual shifts, maintenance and contracts separately.

For a bar, diner or fast-food operating budget, change the revenue mix and account definitions before using the same structure. Keep beverage and food denominators consistent, and separate launch spending from ongoing costs. Preserve the original budget, revise the forecast with evidence and use the dated cash schedule for deposits, supplier payments and tax dates.

FAQs

What belongs in a restaurant monthly budget?

Sales by channel, cost of goods sold, loaded labor, occupancy, owner pay, utilities, marketing and other recurring expenses. Add notes for costs that are one-time or paid on a different schedule.

How do I calculate restaurant break-even from the budget?

Divide monthly fixed costs by contribution per order. In the worked example, $27,000 divided by $16 requires 1,688 whole orders, before a profit target.

Should restaurant payroll be budgeted as a percentage of sales?

Use the actual minimum schedule and employer burden first. A percentage can help compare periods, but it does not tell you what a slow Tuesday shift costs.

What is the difference between budget and forecast?

The budget is the approved target for the period. A forecast is your best current expectation after you learn more; preserving both lets you explain variances.

Can I use last month’s food invoices as COGS?

Not without checking inventory. Beginning inventory plus purchases minus ending inventory is the period cost of goods sold under a consistent inventory method.

Is the downloadable sheet a cash-flow forecast?

No. It compares operating revenue and costs in one month. Plan deposits, debt principal, equipment purchases and timing of collections separately.

Are the restaurant cost percentages recommended budget targets?

No. The cited 2025 National Restaurant Association report describes 2024 survey medians. Use current local costs for your budget; the survey is comparison context, not prescribed targets.

Why does the COGS variance change after adjusting for sales?

At the original 30% rate, $57,000 actual sales allows $17,100 COGS. Actual COGS of $18,700 exceeds that allowance by $1,600, although it is only $700 above the original $18,000 budget. This flex assumes stable prices and mix.
